# Faulty Exception Handling

This example demonstrates a dangerous exception-handling pattern: catching a
broad exception and then doing nothing with it.

The code reads console input and writes it to a file. Under normal conditions
that looks harmless. The problem appears when file creation fails. Instead of
surfacing the I/O error, the application silently swallows it and loops again.

That turns a visible failure into silent non-progress. From a secure-coding
perspective, this matters because availability failures are still security
failures. A service that keeps running but cannot do its job is harder to
detect, diagnose, and recover than one that fails loudly with a clear cause.

## What you will learn

By the end of this example you will understand:

- why `catch (Exception e) {}` is a dangerous default
- how swallowed exceptions can create infinite retry loops or silent data loss
- why exception handling belongs to the control-flow design, not just to logging
- how a fail-fast variant makes the problem visible immediately
- why "the process is still alive" is not evidence that the application is
  healthy

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 21 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)

This example uses the Maven Wrapper (`./mvnw`), so you do not need to install
Maven separately.

The permission-based fault demo below assumes Unix-style `chmod` semantics, so
it works as written on macOS and Linux. On Windows, you may need to reproduce
the same failure by changing directory permissions through the file explorer or
ACL tools instead.

## Inspect the vulnerable implementation

Start with the vulnerable implementation.

The program writes console input to `output/demo.txt` until it sees the
character `Q`. The key design flaw is the outer `while` loop combined with the
empty `catch` block.

What you gain from this step: you see exactly how the swallowed exception
affects control flow.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.exceptions;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public final class App {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(App.class);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        log.info("Hello! Please enter some text:");

        int in = 0;
        while (((char)in) != 'Q') {
            File outputDirectory = new File("output");
            try {
                outputDirectory.mkdir();
                File file = new File(outputDirectory, "demo.txt");

                try (FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream(file)) {
                    for (in = System.in.read(); ((char)in) != 'Q'; in = System.in.read()) {
                        out.write(in);
                    }
                }
            } catch (Exception e) {
                // BUG: swallowing the exception means the application keeps looping
                // even though it can no longer make progress.
                // log.error("error", e);
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The core bug is not just "missing logging". It is that the exception handler
hides a condition the loop cannot recover from. If file creation fails before
any input is read, the variable `in` is never updated, so the loop keeps
spinning and the application stops making progress.

## Run the vulnerable implementation in the happy path

First run the vulnerable program under normal conditions.

We do this before breaking anything so you can see the intended behavior and
confirm what the application is supposed to do when file output is available.

What you gain from this step: a clean baseline for comparison.

```shell
rm -rf 'output'
printf 'hello\nQ\n' | java --class-path 'target/faulty_exception_handler-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar' com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App
printf '\n--- demo.txt ---\n'
cat 'output/demo.txt'
```

Observed output

```
--- demo.txt ---
hello
Apr 08, 2026 8:02:50 PM com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App main
INFO: Hello! Please enter some text:
```

In the happy path, the program behaves as expected:

- it accepts input
- it writes the data to `output/demo.txt`
- it exits when `Q` is encountered

That baseline matters. Secure-coding examples are stronger when the learner
first understands the intended behavior before seeing how the failure mode
breaks it.

## Trigger the swallowed-exception failure manually

Now trigger the fault condition deliberately.

The goal is to make file creation fail before the program reads the next input
character. Because the exception is swallowed, the application will keep
retrying the same failing operation and will never reach the logic that looks
for `Q`.

What you gain from this step: you see how a swallowed exception changes a
straightforward I/O problem into a misleading "hung" process.

Run these commands manually:

```shell
rm 'output/demo.txt'
chmod 555 'output'
java --class-path 'target/faulty_exception_handler-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar' com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App
```

Then type a few characters, including `Q`.

Expected behavior:

- the program prints the initial prompt
- typing `Q` does not terminate the program
- the process appears alive, but it is no longer doing useful work

That is the actual risk: the failure is no longer observable to the caller, and
the application has entered a silent retry loop.

## Restore the directory after the fault demo

Restore normal permissions before moving on.

What you gain from this step: a clean workspace for the remediated run.

```shell
chmod 755 'output'
```

## Inspect the remediated implementation

Now inspect the safer variant.

The fixed version still uses the same overall workflow, but it does not swallow
the I/O failure. Instead, it logs the problem and lets the exception terminate
the program.

What you gain from this step: you see the difference between silent failure and
explicit failure.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.exceptions;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public final class App_fixed {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(App_fixed.class);

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        log.info("Hello! Please enter some text:");

        int in = 0;
        while (((char) in) != 'Q') {
            File outputDirectory = new File("output");
            if (!outputDirectory.exists() && !outputDirectory.mkdir()) {
                throw new IOException("Could not create output directory: " + outputDirectory.getAbsolutePath());
            }

            File file = new File(outputDirectory, "demo.txt");
            try (FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream(file)) {
                for (in = System.in.read(); ((char) in) != 'Q'; in = System.in.read()) {
                    out.write(in);
                }
            } catch (IOException e) {
                log.error("Could not persist console input to {}", file.getAbsolutePath(), e);
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

This version is intentionally simpler from an error-handling perspective:

- it validates the output directory creation path
- it handles only the specific I/O failure it expects at this boundary
- it rethrows the exception instead of pretending the application can continue

That is a much safer contract for callers and operators.

printf 'hello\nQ\n' | java --class-path 'target/faulty_exception_handler-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar' com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App_fixed
printf '\n--- demo.txt ---\n'
cat 'output/demo.txt'

Observed output

Apr 08, 2026 8:02:51 PM com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App_fixed main

## Run the remediated implementation against the same fault

Now reproduce the same unwritable-directory condition, but run the fixed
variant instead.

What you gain from this step: you see the application fail fast with a visible
cause instead of entering a hidden retry loop.

```shell
rm -rf output
mkdir -p output
chmod 555 output
set +e; printf 'Q\n' | java -cp target/faulty_exception_handler-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App_fixed > target/app-fixed.log 2>&1; rc=$?; echo "Java exit status: $rc"; cat target/app-fixed.log; chmod 755 output; test $rc -ne 0
```

Expected failure

```
Java exit status: 1
Apr 08, 2026 8:02:51 PM com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App_fixed main
INFO: Hello! Please enter some text:
Apr 08, 2026 8:02:51 PM com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App_fixed main
SEVERE: Could not persist console input to ./output/demo.txt
java.io.FileNotFoundException: output/demo.txt (Permission denied)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.open0(Native Method)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.open(FileOutputStream.java:255)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.<init>(FileOutputStream.java:210)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.<init>(FileOutputStream.java:171)
    at com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App_fixed.main(App_fixed.java:24)

Exception in thread "main" java.io.FileNotFoundException: output/demo.txt (Permission denied)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.open0(Native Method)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.open(FileOutputStream.java:255)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.<init>(FileOutputStream.java:210)
    at java.base/java.io.FileOutputStream.<init>(FileOutputStream.java:171)
    at com.oracle.jsc.exceptions.App_fixed.main(App_fixed.java:24)
```

This is the behavior you want in a secure system:

- the failure is visible immediately
- the operator gets a concrete error instead of a "stuck" process
- the application does not continue pretending it can still process input

In other words, the fixed version fails closed instead of failing silently.

## Cleanup

Remove the demo output directory when you are finished.

```shell
chmod 755 'output' || true
rm -rf 'output'
```

## What this example teaches

- Broad, silent exception handling can be worse than no handling because it
  hides real failures.
- Exception handling is part of control-flow design, not just an afterthought
  for logging.
- A process that remains alive but cannot make progress is an operational
  hazard.
- Fail-fast behavior with a visible root cause is often safer than silent retry.
- Secure coding includes preserving observability when something goes wrong.
